defects.before: - One loop pass of these three loops moves 256 B with 8 `ldp` or `stp` instructions. Each instruction moves two 16-byte registers.
defects.after: - One loop pass of each of these three loops moves 256 B. The read loop has 8 `ldp` instructions. The write loop has 8 `stp` instructions. The copy loop has 8 `ldp` and 8 `stp` instructions. Each of these instructions moves two 16-byte registers.
defects.evidence: The copy loop of DEF_ASMCOPY (source lines 707 to 722, listing.txt lines 107 to 122) has 8 ldp plus 8 stp per loop pass, which is 16 instructions and not 8.

defects.before: - The two loops differ in four points. Register numbers: q0 to q15 here, q31 to q16 in `k_read`. Save of d8 to d15: only here.
defects.after: - The two functions differ in four points. Register numbers: q0 to q15 here, q31 to q16 in `k_read`. Save of d8 to d15, outside the loop: only here.
defects.evidence: In listing.txt the 4 stp and 4 ldp of d8 to d15 of k_asmread stand at 0x4ac0 to 0x4ad0 and 0x4b00 to 0x4b0c, outside the loop 0x4ad4 to 0x4afc, so the save is a difference of the functions and not of the loops.

defects.before: - The clobber list names only v0 to v3. The calling rules do not oblige a function to keep these registers.
defects.after: - Of the vector registers, the clobber list names only v0 to v3. The calling rules do not require a function to keep these registers.
defects.evidence: Source line 1003 is `: "v0", "v1", "v2", "v3", "memory", "cc"`, so the list also names memory and cc, and "oblige" is an uncommon word.

defects.before: - This text fixes the unrolling: 8 `ldp` per loop pass. gcc passes assembler text on without a change.
defects.after: - The unrolling is part of this text: 8 `ldp` per loop pass. gcc passes assembler text on without a change.
defects.evidence: "fixes" can be read as "repairs", and the intended meaning is that the assembler text itself holds the 8 ldp per loop pass (source lines 624 to 631).

defects.before: These lines define all 17 kernels of lines 500 to 849 from the stand-in macros, also `k_read`, `k_write` and `k_copy`.
defects.after: These lines define all 17 kernels of lines 500 to 849 from the stand-in macros. The 17 include `k_read`, `k_write` and `k_copy`.
defects.evidence: Source lines 880 to 896 hold exactly 17 macro uses and read, write and copy are 3 of them, so "also" could be read as 17 plus 3.

defects.before: - The comment describes the read_pf kernels: the asmread loop plus four prefetch instructions per loop pass, one per 64 B line.
defects.after: - The comment describes the read_pf kernels: the asmread loop plus four prefetch instructions per loop pass, one per 64 B line. A line here is a block of 64 B of memory (a cache line).
defects.evidence: This row is the first use of "64 B line" in the chunk, and the term was defined only later, in the row of lines 984 to 988.

defects.before: - So one loop pass loads 64 B of the 256 B that it walks: the bytes 0 to 15 of each 64 B line.
defects.after: - So one loop pass loads 64 B of its block of 256 B: the bytes 0 to 15 of each 64 B line.
defects.evidence: "walks" is a metaphor (plain-English rule 1), and the same row already uses the literal term "the current block of 256 B".

defects.before: That is 7 instructions per 256 B walked [Ref1].
defects.after: That is 7 instructions per block of 256 B [Ref1].
defects.evidence: Same metaphor "walked"; the count of 7 instructions per loop pass is confirmed by listing.txt lines 757 to 763.

defects.before: (no heading; the row stood under the heading "`DEF_ASMREAD(asmread, 0)`: the kernel `asmread` of the test")
defects.after: heading added: "`asmread2` and `read_nop4` to `read_nop32` (not run by the test)"

defects.before: `main` rejects any other value of `--bytes` and any other size of a `--seq` entry (lines 2973 and 2991).
defects.after: `main` ends the program with status 2 when `--bytes` is 0 or is not a multiple of 256 B (line 2973). It does the same when the size of a `--seq` entry is not a multiple of 256 B (line 2991).
defects.evidence: Lines 2973 and 2991 of bwx12.c call usage(), which ends with exit(2) (line 1747); line 2989 replaces an entry size of 0 by the --bytes value, so "rejects any other size" did not say what the check does.

defects.before: gcc passes assembler text on without a change.
defects.after: gcc does not change the instructions of assembler text. It only puts register names in the places of `%[p]` and `%[end]`.
defects.evidence: The source text holds `%[p]` and `%[end]` (lines 624 to 634) and the listing holds x0 and x1 in their places (listing.txt lines 66 to 75), so the text is changed in the operands and only the instructions are kept.

defects.before: objdump prints `b.cc` for this branch and names `b.lo` as another name of it [Ref1].
defects.after: The listing prints `b.cc` for this branch and names `b.lo` as another name of it [Ref1].
defects.evidence: The program name objdump is defined neither in chunk 1 nor in the word list of the overview, while "the listing" is the term that the rows of this companion use for Ref1.

defects.before: End test: `cmp x0, x1` with `b.cc` here, `cmp x1, x0` with `b.hi` in `k_read` [Ref1].
defects.after: End test: `cmp x0, x1` with `b.cc` here, `cmp x1, x0` with `b.hi` in `k_read` [Ref1]. Both end tests branch back while the pointer is below `end`.
defects.evidence: In listing.txt x0 is the pointer and x1 is the end in both functions, so `cmp x0, x1` with `b.cc` (unsigned lower) and `cmp x1, x0` with `b.hi` (unsigned higher) are the same condition; the row listed the two forms as a difference without saying so.

defects.before: moves the write pointer on by 32 words / both pointers move on by 256 B / `add` moves the read pointer on by 256 B (5 places)
defects.after: moves the write pointer forward by 32 words / both pointers move forward by 256 B / `add` moves the read pointer forward by 256 B (5 places)
defects.evidence: "move on by" is a phrasal verb that a non-native reader must guess; chunk 1 of the same companion writes "moves the read position forward by" for the same step.

defects.after: The listing shows the `dup` and `stp` instructions of this function [Ref1]. `dup` copies one 8-byte value into both halves of a 16-byte vector register.
defects.evidence: This row is the first use of the instruction name `dup`; chunk 1 and the word list of the overview do not define it, and this chunk explained it only later, in the row of lines 671 to 697 (listing.txt line 19: `dup v31.2d, x2`).

defects.after: Machine code before the loop: `dup v31.2d, x2` (x2 holds `v`) and `add x1, x0, x1, lsl #3` [Ref1].

defects.after: For these three kernels the pad is 0 bytes (lines 214, 1057 and 1135).

defects.after: Before each interval of this kernel one call covers the whole buffer: the warm-up pass (line 1669).
